gapTheirs: Over-loaded page: 86.0% of ink is chromatic, leaving only four short function words (`You`, `which`, `with`, `it`) plus `you`/`a` in neutral #191919 — line 3 runs three reds in a row (`clutter`, `Style`, `Check`, 173+123+124 px) with no black between them, so the neutral spine that normally tells the eye where a marked word begins is gone and the row reads as one continuous highlighter stripe.
verdict: Put these side by side and the colours are the same colours — same blue, same rust, same ochre, same plum, same green, to the hex — so this comes down to which page's colour you can trust. A's doesn't hold: `verbs` is red and `repetitions`, two words later, is black; `clutter` is black and `writer` is red; `Style Check` arrives half red and half blue, which stops you mid-line to work out whether the app means something by it. B's page is nearly all colour and line 3 is three reds with nothing black to break them, which is tiring — but it is at least consistent, and consistency is what makes a highlight readable as information instead of decoration.

states.name: all-dark
states.gap: B drops two head nouns out of body ink into nothing: 'repetitions' and 'clutter' render #CCCCCC while their coordinate partner 'verbs' and every other object noun render #CE896D — so 'weak verbs' reads gold+red and the parallel 'unwanted repetitions' reads gold+grey, adjective marked, head noun blank. B also paints 'spot' in 'helps you spot weak verbs' noun-red #CE896D where A paints it verb-blue #829EBF.
states.gapTheirs: Colour saturation of the line: A's line 2 carries hue on 1086 of 1173 px of ink span (93%), leaving only 'you' (71 px) and two commas in body #CCCCCC — 8095 noun-red pixels vs B's 5035, and only 3337 body-grey vs B's 5595. When 93% of a line is painted, the highlight stops discriminating and reads as wallpaper rather than a diagnostic.
states.verdict: On the rows this piece is actually judged by these two are the same page — the five hues match to the byte, the contraction splits the same way with the apostrophe on the verb side, the punctuation stays plain on both, and the left margin lands on the same column. What separates them is what gets painted, and B's holes fall in the worst possible place: it marks 'unwanted' but not 'repetitions', 'eliminate' but not 'clutter', so grey stops meaning 'ordinary word' and starts meaning 'the tagger shrugged' — and once absence of colour is untrustworthy the tool is dead. A's sin is the opposite and lesser one: it paints 93% of line 2, which is loud and near-useless as a filter, but at least it is uniformly loud and you can learn to read past it. A writer trimming this passage would sooner squint through A's excess than second-guess every grey word in B.

states.name: focus-sentence
states.gap: A breaks the two-word name 'Style Check' across two Categories — 'Style' at #BB512A, 'Check' at #4675B5 — so the blue on the page is no longer only the verbs; B keeps both words at #BB512A and leaves blue to `'ll make` alone. Secondarily A lays down ~7% less coloured ink at identical hue (blue 'make' coverage 636 vs 691, brown 'persuasive' 1668 vs 1814), so its 4.4:1 blue and 4.5:1 brown sit that much nearer the 1.6:1 dim grey.
states.gapTheirs: B's caret is #36BFFA over a 7px antialiased body with a #6BA7D4 halo, against A's 444 pixels of hard-edged #00BFFF at exactly 6px — a softer, greyer, less locatable bar that sits 2px off the final 'e' of 'more'. Set against the row this piece is actually judged on, B gives up nothing: same five hexes, same dim, same split.
states.verdict: On the row that is actually being judged this is a dead heat, and I'd rather say so than invent a winner: five Category hexes match to the byte on both sides, both dim rows carry one flat #C6C4C2 with no residual red or purple anywhere in ~25k ink pixels, and both cut `it'll` at the same seam with the apostrophe carried into the verb blue. What separates them is one word — A paints 'Check' blue, B paints it red — and while the tag itself is the shipped tagger's business, the page a writer looks at is not: in B the blue ink is the verbs and nothing else, which is the entire promise of the feature, whereas in A a proper noun wears the verb colour and the signal muddies. That plus B's marginally denser stroke, which keeps the blue and brown from drifting toward the dim grey, is the whole margin. Anyone who picks A here is picking a crisper caret, and the caret is not this row.
